title: Field Notes: The AgentCore Memory write that returns success and reads back empty
summary:
# Summary

The author discovered two operational gotchas when implementing long-term memory in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore: a non-existent API method that passed code review despite never being called, and a critical read-after-write consistency issue where `BatchCreateMemoryRecords` returns `201` but the record remains unsearchable in its namespace for 15-30 seconds. The post provides practical guidance on verifying actual SDK operations, understanding the two-tier memory architecture, and building robust read patterns that account for eventual consistency rather than relying on fixed delays.

title: Every dashboard was green while the agent burned six figures a year
summary:
# Summary

This post describes a costly failure mode where an AI agent ran in an infinite loop for days while returning successful responses, remaining invisible to standard monitoring. The author explains five specific conditions that cause agent runaways (context bloat, unsatisfiable goals, model regeneration, broken tools, and external re-drives) and recommends both hard operational bounds on loop iterations and custom instrumentation to catch these failures—particularly per-session metrics that would surface a single stuck session against normal baselines.

title: The LLM is not a security boundary
summary: This post explains how to architect an AI agent system handling sensitive data by treating the language model as fundamentally untrustworthy and building deterministic security controls outside the model itself. The author argues that no single control is flawless, so the solution is layered defense-in-depth with ranked, load-bearing deterministic controls closest to the data and probabilistic safeguards as a backstop. The post details specific implementation patterns for identity verification, ACL filtering at retrieval time, tool allowlisting, and query validation to prevent both accidental model errors and prompt injection attacks from compromised data.

title: Your LLM security diagram defends the wrong layer
summary:
# Summary

The standard LLM security diagram showing four attack types (prompt injection, retrieval poisoning, context poisoning, output injection) with mitigations at each stage is misleading because it treats these as separate threats requiring probabilistic classifiers at each layer—an approach that creates "four leaky nets stacked on top of each other" rather than a real boundary. The author argues that effective defense requires moving security enforcement to a deterministic layer where the system validates proposed actions against a finite, enumerable set of allowed operations (tools, tables, entitlements, destinations) keyed to a verified principal, treating input/output classifiers as backstops rather than primary controls.

title: Part 1: Intent vs State. How AWS DevOps Agent Closes the Gap Between What Your System Is and What You Decided It Should Be
summary:
# Summary

This post introduces a framework for closing a gap in AI-powered incident response: while current tools excel at analyzing system state (logs, metrics, traces), they miss organizational intent (ADRs, runbooks, decisions). The author describes an architecture using AWS DevOps Agent with a custom MCP server that retrieves organizational decisions from a knowledge base, enabling agents to correlate telemetry with documented commitments—like identifying when an incident stems from a missed deadline rather than a recent code change. The series will walk through building this system, starting with the conceptual framing and progressing to implementation details.

title: Part 1: Why I Chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (And What Lambda Gets Wrong for AI Agents)
summary:
# Summary

This post explains why the author chose Amazon Bedrock AgentCore over Lambda for building a production AI agent, detailing how Lambda's limitations (15-minute timeout, stateless design, session management complexity, VPC cold starts) make it unsuitable for conversational AI workloads. AgentCore is a managed container orchestrator that handles session routing, memory persistence, and streaming natively, though it requires understanding its session model and has less mature tooling than Lambda. The author outlines a six-part series documenting the full production setup, from architecture decisions through cost optimization, with a companion demo repository.

title: Part 2: The MCP Server: Turning ADRs and Incidents into a Queryable Org-Knowledge Surface
summary:
# Summary

This post explains how the author built an MCP server to give a DevOps agent access to organizational intent through a typed query layer over documented decisions, rather than embedding all context in the system prompt. The MCP exposes four tools that query a Bedrock Knowledge Base containing ADRs and other decision documents, with structured frontmatter fields enabling deterministic filtering on metadata like expiration dates and service ownership. The design prioritizes structured outputs and exact filters over semantic search alone, ensuring the agent cites specific, verifiable information rather than paraphrasing.

title: Part 2: CDK Infrastructure for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore (And Every Gotcha You'll Hit)
summary:
# Summary

This post documents nine specific pitfalls when deploying AWS AgentCore using CDK, including naming restrictions (no hyphens), ECR repository timing issues, missing CDK constructs for logging configuration, VPC endpoint conflicts, KMS key policy requirements, security group rule representation in tests, mandatory parameters for runtime updates, Memory resource rollback failures, and array matching order sensitivity in CDK assertions. The author provides code examples and recovery procedures for each gotcha, along with a testing strategy using snapshot tests and targeted assertions.

title: Part 3: Wiring It Into AWS DevOps Agent: AgentSpace, register-service, and the IAM Trust Policy That Ate My Afternoon
summary:
# Summary

This post walks through integrating an MCP Lambda with AWS DevOps Agent using CDK, focusing on the IAM and deployment challenges. The author demonstrates a three-stack architecture (KnowledgeBase, MCP Server, DevOps Agent) and highlights three non-obvious IAM gotchas encountered during implementation, plus a production OIDC issue discovered while deploying the blog post itself.

title: Part 3: Building the AI Agent with Strands Agents SDK, Prompt Caching, and AgentCore Memory
summary:
# Summary

This post details building a Python agent application that runs within the CDK infrastructure, using the Strands Agents SDK to create a Bedrock-backed reasoning loop with AgentCore Memory integration and Bedrock Guardrails. The author explains why Strands was chosen over LangChain (AWS-native design, simpler tool definitions, active development alignment with AgentCore), covers the dual-model strategy using Claude Sonnet 4.5 for primary conversations and Amazon Nova Pro for background tasks, and highlights prompt caching as a major cost optimization that achieves 90% savings on cached tokens. The implementation includes tool definitions as decorated functions, AgentCore Memory for persistent context across sessions, adaptive retry configuration for handling Bedrock throttling, and a streaming agent loop that forwards responses via Server-Sent Events while storing conversation turns in memory.

title: Part 4: Running Your AgentCore Agent Locally with Docker (The Right Way)
summary:
# Summary

This post explains how to locally test a Docker-based agent before deploying to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, emphasizing the critical requirement to build with `--platform linux/amd64` to ensure compatibility with AgentCore's x86_64-only runtime. It covers the Dockerfile setup, environment configuration via `.env.local`, running the container with AWS credentials mounted, and testing the health check and invoke endpoints with curl, while noting that Apple Silicon Macs will experience slower builds due to QEMU emulation.

title: Part 5: CI/CD for Bedrock AgentCore with GitHub Actions and AWS OIDC (No Stored Credentials)
summary:
# Summary

This post explains why OIDC is superior to stored AWS access keys for GitHub Actions CI/CD and provides a complete setup guide. It covers creating an IAM OIDC provider, configuring trust policies scoped to specific repositories, building and pushing Docker images with dual tags for easy rollback, and integrating with AWS Bedrock AgentCore for automated deployments with multi-environment promotion support.

title: Part 6: Cost & Performance for Bedrock AgentCore: Prompt Caching, Model Selection, and CloudWatch Alarms
summary:
# Summary

This post covers cost optimization strategies for production AgentCore deployments on AWS, emphasizing that Bedrock model invocations are the dominant cost driver. The author details how prompt caching (caching system prompts and tool definitions) can save approximately $480/month on a moderately-used system, and recommends using cheaper models like Amazon Nova Pro for classification and summarization tasks instead of Claude Sonnet 4.5 for everything. The post also provides CloudWatch alarms to catch runaway costs, lifecycle configuration guidance, and estimates total monthly costs at $150-240 for a 500-conversation-per-day agent.

title: Field Notes: Turning prompt caching on for a production Bedrock workload
summary:
# Summary

This post explains how to enable and verify prompt caching in AWS Bedrock's `BedrockModel`, a feature that reduces costs by caching system prompts and tool registries. The author reveals that caching is disabled by default despite being available via two kwargs, documents a per-model gotcha where Amazon Nova rejects tool caching while Anthropic models accept it, and provides a measurement technique using the per-call `usage` block to verify cache hits in seconds rather than waiting for CloudWatch metrics. Measured results show hit ratios of 99.9% on Nova Pro and 99.8% on Sonnet 4.6, translating to 55% and 78% billing reductions respectively on system-prefix tokens.

title: Field Notes: Three things I learned diagnosing a production Bedrock workload
summary:
# Summary

This post documents three production lessons from diagnosing an AWS Bedrock AI workload: load tests can mask throttling exceptions invisible to higher-level metrics, latency decomposition reveals that time-to-first-token accounts for significant delays beyond model generation speed, and prompt caching is rarely enabled despite being a simple configuration change that dramatically reduces costs. The author provides specific CloudWatch metrics and measurements to support each lesson and explains how to detect and fix each issue.

title: What a Year 10 study system taught me about production AI failure modes
summary:
# Summary

The author built a tutoring system for his son using Claude projects and Cowork, iterating through three versions before arriving at a working architecture that aggregates weekly tutoring sessions into differentiated emails for different stakeholders. The key insight was inverting the data flow from pull-based (reading project chats) to push-based (having projects emit session summaries to Gmail) after discovering the initial design's assumptions about API capabilities were incorrect. The five lessons—verify primitives before designing, prefer push over pull architectures, embrace human-in-the-loop workflows, use calibration windows before full deployment, and maintain decision logs—apply directly to production AWS AI work and represent stack-agnostic architectural disciplines that determine whether AI agents succeed or fail in enterprise settings.
